p01-who-fails-title.name: p01-who-fails-title
p01-who-fails-title.text: First find who is wrong: use the "labeled score" m: y·g

p01-who-fails-ctx.name: p01-who-fails-ctx
p01-who-fails-ctx.text: Eight points: blue circles are the positive class ($y=+1$), red triangles the negative class ($y=-1$). The current boundary is $\mathbf v_0=(1,1,-0.5)$, that is $g=x_1+x_2-0.5$.

p01-who-fails-src.name: p01-who-fails-src
p01-who-fails-src.text: Source: KP01 main-example boundary; the eight points are the lecture's web-demo data, not claimed to be the textbook figure's raw data.

p01-who-fails-c0.name: p01-who-fails-c0
p01-who-fails-c0.text: Some points are on the wrong side of the line. How can one number tell "correct" from "wrong" at once?

p01-who-fails-c1.name: p01-who-fails-c1
p01-who-fails-c1.text: Labeled score $m_i=y_i\,g_i$: the score times the true label. $m_i>0$ means the score and label have the same sign (correct); $m_i\le0$ means wrong, or exactly on the line (this lecture also counts it as needing correction).

p01-who-fails-c3.name: p01-who-fails-c3
p01-who-fails-c3.text: The other six points have $m$ between $0.6$ and $1.2$, all correct. The set needing correction is $Y=\{A,B\}$.

p01-who-fails-c4.name: p01-who-fails-c4
p01-who-fails-c4.text: Only the points in $Y$ ask for a correction.

p02-augment-title.name: p02-augment-title
p02-augment-title.text: Put the intercept b into the vector too: add a feature that is always 1

p02-augment-ctx.name: p02-augment-ctx
p02-augment-ctx.text: To write "a wrong point's request" as a vector addition, first make the score $g=\mathbf w^T\mathbf x+b$ a single inner product. Take A as an example.

p02-augment-src.name: p02-augment-src
p02-augment-src.text: Source: KP02 lecture §1.1 (augmented vectors); the numbers of A and $\mathbf v_0$ come from the lecture's original Example 3.1.

p02-augment-c0.name: p02-augment-c0
p02-augment-c0.text: $\mathbf w^T\mathbf x+b$ has an extra "+b", so it is not a pure inner product. Can $b$ become "just another weight"?

p02-augment-sum.name: p02-augment-sum
p02-augment-sum.text: Add: $0.4+0.05+(-0.5)=-0.05=\mathbf v^T\mathbf a=g$. The position of $b$ is multiplied by the cell that is always $1$.

p02-augment-c5.name: p02-augment-c5
p02-augment-c5.text: After augmenting, $g=\mathbf v^T\mathbf a$ is just one inner product. From now on every point is written $\mathbf a_i=(\mathbf x_i,1)$ and the weights always $\mathbf v=(\mathbf w,b)$.

p02-augment-c6.name: p02-augment-c6
p02-augment-c6.text: What matters: correcting one point only requires adding $\pm\mathbf a_i$ to $\mathbf v$, which corrects both $\mathbf w$ and $b$. The next page uses this.

p03-one-point-title.name: p03-one-point-title
p03-one-point-title.text: Fix only A: A becomes correct, but B gets worse

p03-one-point-ctx.name: p03-one-point-ctx
p03-one-point-ctx.text: Correcting one wrong point $i$: $\mathbf v\leftarrow\mathbf v+\rho\,y_i\,\mathbf a_i$. Learning rate $\rho=0.7$. See the boundary and the two scores after correcting A.

p03-one-point-src.name: p03-one-point-src
p03-one-point-src.text: Source: KP02 lecture §1.1 update rule; "fix only A" is a teaching contrast chosen before returning to batch; numbers computed by build_kp02_en.py.

p03-one-point-c0.name: p03-one-point-c0
p03-one-point-c0.text: Look only at A (positive): it asks to add $+\mathbf a_A$ to $\mathbf v$. If only A is fixed, where does the boundary move? What happens to B?

p03-one-point-c1.name: p03-one-point-c1
p03-one-point-c1.text: $\mathbf v^{(A)}=(1,1,-0.5)+0.7(0.4,0.05,1)=(1.28,1.035,0.2)$. The orange line is the new boundary.

p03-one-point-c2.name: p03-one-point-c2
p03-one-point-c2.text: A's score $-0.05\to0.7638$, an increase of exactly $\rho\|\mathbf a_A\|^2=0.7\times1.1625=0.81375$. A is now correct.

p03-one-point-c3.name: p03-one-point-c3
p03-one-point-c3.text: B's (negative class) $m$ goes from $-0.05$ to $-0.7202$: even worse. The other six points keep positive $m$.

p03-one-point-c4.name: p03-one-point-c4
p03-one-point-c4.text: Fixing points one at a time makes them pull against each other: fixing one can make another worse. So we switch to "add up everyone's requests first".

p04-sum-title.name: p04-sum-title
p04-sum-title.text: The batch way: add up y·a of every point in Y first

p04-sum-ctx.name: p04-sum-ctx
p04-sum-ctx.text: Each wrong point asks to add $y_i\mathbf a_i$: positive points add $+\mathbf a$, negative points add $-\mathbf a$. First see the vector sum of the first two components ($x_1,x_2$ directions).

p04-sum-src.name: p04-sum-src
p04-sum-src.text: Source: In the lecture's original Example 3.1, $\sum\delta_i\mathbf a_i=(-0.6,0.7,0)$ ($\delta=-y$); this page uses $\sum y\mathbf a=(0.6,-0.7,0)$, differing by a sign, so the update rule is equivalent.

p04-sum-c0.name: p04-sum-c0
p04-sum-c0.text: A is positive: it requests $+\mathbf a_A$. B is negative: it requests $-\mathbf a_B$ (opposite direction). Place the two arrows head to tail and look at the sum.

p04-sum-c1.name: p04-sum-c1
p04-sum-c1.text: A: $y_A\mathbf a_A=(0.4,0.05,1)$, the first two components as the blue arrow.

p04-sum-c2.name: p04-sum-c2
p04-sum-c2.text: B: $y_B\mathbf a_B=-(-0.2,0.75,1)=(0.2,-0.75,-1)$, drawn from the tip of the blue arrow.

p04-sum-c3.name: p04-sum-c3
p04-sum-c3.text: Sum $\sum y\mathbf a=(0.6,-0.7,0)$: the gold arrow is the combined force of the two requests.

p04-sum-c4.name: p04-sum-c4
p04-sum-c4.text: Third component (intercept): $+1$ and $-1$ cancel exactly, so the intercept does not change. This is a coincidence of this example, not a general rule.

p04-sum-c5.name: p04-sum-c5
p04-sum-c5.text: Batch update: $\mathbf v_1=\mathbf v_0+\rho\sum_{i\in Y}y_i\mathbf a_i$, where $\rho=0.7$ is the step size.

p05-update-title.name: p05-update-title
p05-update-title.text: Update v with the combined force: are A and B now both correct?

p05-update-ctx.name: p05-update-ctx
p05-update-ctx.text: $\mathbf v_1=\mathbf v_0+\rho\sum y\mathbf a$. Draw the new boundary and substitute A and B to check.

p05-update-src.name: p05-update-src
p05-update-src.text: Source: KP02 lecture original Example 3.1: $\mathbf v_1=(1.42,0.51,-0.5)$, new scores $0.0935$ and $-0.4015$; numbers recomputed by build_kp02_en.py.

p05-update-c0.name: p05-update-c0
p05-update-c0.text: Predict first: with $\rho=0.7$ adding the combined force, will the new boundary classify both A and B correctly? Will it break the other six points?

p05-update-c2.name: p05-update-c2
p05-update-c2.text: The green line is the new boundary; the gray dashed line is the old one. See which side of the new line A and B are on.

p05-update-c4.name: p05-update-c4
p05-update-c4.text: A and B are on the correct side; the other six points are also on the correct side (numbers on the next page). One batch update classifies all eight points correctly.

p06-stop-title.name: p06-stop-title
p06-stop-title.text: After the update, how do we know to stop? Check whether Y is empty

p06-stop-ctx.name: p06-stop-ctx
p06-stop-ctx.text: Compare each point's labeled score $m=y\,g$ before and after the update.

p06-stop-src.name: p06-stop-src
p06-stop-src.text: Source: KP02 lecture §1.2 and [correction]: the stopping condition is $Y=\emptyset$; $J=0$ is not enough to stop (counterexample $\mathbf v=\mathbf 0$).

p06-stop-c0.name: p06-stop-c0
p06-stop-c0.text: The red region is $m\le0$. After the update, where do the $m$ of A and B go? And the other six points?

p06-stop-c1.name: p06-stop-c1
p06-stop-c1.text: Before: A and B are in the red region ($Y=\{A,B\}$), the other six are in the green region.

p06-stop-c2.name: p06-stop-c2
p06-stop-c2.text: A: $-0.05\to0.0935$; B: $-0.05\to0.4015$. Both leave the red region.

p06-stop-c3.name: p06-stop-c3
p06-stop-c3.text: The other six points have $m$ from $0.613$ to $1.25$, all positive. The red region holds no points: $Y=\emptyset$, so we can stop.

p06-stop-c4.name: p06-stop-c4
p06-stop-c4.text: Two warnings: (1) one update does not guarantee fewer errors; look at the new $Y$. (2) loss $J=0$ is not enough to stop: at $\mathbf v=\mathbf 0$ all scores and $J$ are $0$, yet no point is strictly correct. So the stopping condition is $Y=\emptyset$.

p07-practice-title.name: p07-practice-title
p07-practice-title.text: Practice: change the learning rate to ρ = 0.5. Will A and B still be corrected?

p07-practice-ctx.name: p07-practice-ctx
p07-practice-ctx.text: Same eight points and $\mathbf v_0$. Work it out first: reuse the total correction $(0.6,-0.7,0)$ and only change the factor in front. Press Next when done.

p07-practice-src.name: p07-practice-src
p07-practice-src.text: Source: KP02 lecture practice; answer computed by build_kp02_en.py (v=(1.3,0.65,$−0.5$), new scores 0.0525 and $−0.2725$) and recomputed independently by check_numbers_kp02.py.

p07-practice-q.name: p07-practice-q
p07-practice-q.text: Change the learning rate to $\rho=0.5$. (a) What is the new $\mathbf v$? (b) The new scores of A and B? (c) Is $Y$ empty after one update? (The green line is the $\rho=0.7$ result, for comparison.)

p07-practice-a3.name: p07-practice-a3
p07-practice-a3.text: (c) A is positive, B negative, the other points keep their sign: all $m$ are positive, $Y=\emptyset$. The orange line ($\rho=0.5$) turns by a smaller angle than the green line ($\rho=0.7$) but also classifies all eight points correctly.

p08-summary-title.name: p08-summary-title
p08-summary-title.text: Summary: who fails, add up the requests, update, check

p08-summary-ctx.name: p08-summary-ctx
p08-summary-ctx.text: Recall along the main example; the five conclusions of this KP are on the right.

p08-summary-e0.name: p08-summary-e0
p08-summary-e0.text: Points with $m_i=y_ig_i\le0$ form $Y$; $\mathbf a=(\mathbf x,1)$, $\mathbf v=(\mathbf w,b)$ make $g=\mathbf v^T\mathbf a$

p08-summary-e1.name: p08-summary-e1
p08-summary-e1.text: Fixing one point pulls: fixing A makes B worse

p08-summary-e2.name: p08-summary-e2
p08-summary-e2.text: Batch: $\mathbf v\leftarrow\mathbf v+\rho\sum_{i\in Y}y_i\mathbf a_i$ (positive adds, negative subtracts)

p08-summary-e3.name: p08-summary-e3
p08-summary-e3.text: Stop when $Y=\emptyset$; $J=0$ is not enough, and one update does not guarantee fewer errors

p08-summary-e4.name: p08-summary-e4
p08-summary-e4.text: Open question: if the data is separable, will this repeated update ever stop? Next KP: the convergence proof

p08-loss-title.text: Where does the update rule come from? The perceptron cost and its subgradient
p08-loss-title.name: p08-loss-title

p08-loss-ctx.text: The batch update $\mathbf v\leftarrow\mathbf v+\rho\sum_{i\in Y}y_i\mathbf a_i$ is not arbitrary: it is gradient descent on the perceptron cost $J$.
p08-loss-ctx.name: p08-loss-ctx

p08-loss-src.text: Source: KP02 lecture §1.1 (formal definitions of $Y$ and $J$, and the subgradient); numbers reuse the main example $\mathbf v_0=(1,1,-0.5)$, $\rho=0.7$, recomputed independently. Added page: the original deck left this derivation out, restored from the lecture.
p08-loss-src.name: p08-loss-src

p08-loss-c0.text: Goal: make every point labeled score $m_i=y_i\mathbf v^T\mathbf a_i$ greater than $0$. Only points with $m_i\le0$ pay a cost, with loss $\ell(m)=\max(0,-m)$ per point.
p08-loss-c0.name: p08-loss-c0

p08-loss-f0.text: $J(\mathbf v)=\sum_i\max(0,-y_i\mathbf v^T\mathbf a_i)=\sum_{i\in Y(\mathbf v)}\delta_i\,\mathbf v^T\mathbf a_i,\quad\delta_i=-y_i$
p08-loss-f0.name: p08-loss-f0

p08-loss-c1.text: Both $A$ and $B$ have $m=-0.05$ and each pays $0.05$: $J(\mathbf v_0)=0.05+0.05=0.10$. The other six points have $m>0$ and pay nothing.
p08-loss-c1.name: p08-loss-c1

p08-loss-c2.text: While $Y$ stays fixed, $J$ is linear in $\mathbf v$ with gradient $\nabla J=\sum_{i\in Y}\delta_i\mathbf a_i=-\sum_{i\in Y}y_i\mathbf a_i$. At the kink ($m=0$) this vector is a valid subgradient and still a usable descent direction.
p08-loss-c2.name: p08-loss-c2

p08-loss-c3.text: Step along the negative gradient: $\mathbf v\leftarrow\mathbf v-\rho\nabla J=\mathbf v+\rho\sum_{i\in Y}y_i\mathbf a_i$, exactly the batch update. Here $\nabla J=-(0.6,-0.7,0)$ and $\mathbf v_1=(1,1,-0.5)+0.7(0.6,-0.7,0)=(1.42,0.51,-0.5)$.
p08-loss-c3.name: p08-loss-c3

p08-loss-c4.text: After the update, $m$ for $A$ and $B$ becomes $0.0935$ and $0.4015$, both on the flat part where $\ell=0$: $J(\mathbf v_1)=0$, $Y=\emptyset$, stop.
p08-loss-c4.name: p08-loss-c4

p08-loss-c5.text: Do not use $J=0$ as the stopping rule: at $\mathbf v=\mathbf 0$ every $m=0$ and $J=0$, yet no point is strictly correct. Stop when $Y=\emptyset$ (all $m>0$).
p08-loss-c5.name: p08-loss-c5

p08-loss-cue0.text: First, the goal and formula: the definition of $J$.
p08-loss-cue0.name: p08-loss-cue0

p08-loss-cue1.text: See the blue polyline and red dots: $A$ and $B$ each pay $0.05$.
p08-loss-cue1.name: p08-loss-cue1

p08-loss-cue2.text: See the purple note: gradient and subgradient.
p08-loss-cue2.name: p08-loss-cue2

p08-loss-cue3.text: See the gold formula: one negative-gradient step is the batch update.
p08-loss-cue3.name: p08-loss-cue3

p08-loss-cue4.text: See the green dots: after the update $J$ drops to $0$.
p08-loss-cue4.name: p08-loss-cue4

p08-loss-cue5.text: See the gold star and red warning: $J=0$ is not the stopping rule.
p08-loss-cue5.name: p08-loss-cue5
